questions.q: A 2-week-old female neonate presents with recurrent crops of tense, clear vesicles and bullae in a linear, whorled distribution on the extremities and trunk. Which molecular pathway defect explains the pathophysiology of this condition?
opts: Impaired NF-κB activation leading to failure of TNF-α-induced apoptosis protection in keratinocytes
Autoimmune destruction of basal membrane antigens with circulating IgG antibodies
Defective tight junction proteins causing transiently increased epidermal permeability
Impaired calcium signaling in melanocytes resulting in abnormal pigment distribution
questions.exp: Incontinentia pigmenti (IP) is caused by mutations in the IKBKG gene (NEMO gene) on chromosome Xq28. The IKBKG protein activates the NF-κB pathway, which protects cells against TNF-α-induced apoptosis. In IP, mutant keratinocytes cannot activate this protective complex and undergo spontaneous apoptosis, explaining the vesiculobullous stage.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: A NEMO clownfish swims through castle corridors frantically searching for NF-κB armor—without it, TNF-α dragons torch the keratinocyte knights into apoptotic ash at Xq28.

questions.q: A 7-year-old girl presents with progressive hair loss, milky-white thickened nails, and palmoplantar keratoderma. Her parents report normal sweating and developmentally normal teeth. Which gene mutation is responsible for this condition?
opts: EDAR gene encoding ectodysplasin A receptor
GJB6 gene encoding Connexin 30
EDA gene encoding ectodysplasin A
KRT5 gene encoding keratin 5
questions.exp: Hidrotic Ectodermal Dysplasia (Clouston Syndrome) is caused by autosomal dominant mutations in the GJB6 gene, which encodes Connexin 30, a gap junction protein critical for intercellular communication in ectodermal appendages. The presence of normal sweating and normal teeth specifically distinguishes this from other forms of ectodermal dysplasia caused by different genetic mutations.

questions.q: Which histological finding on skin biopsy from a patient with Hidrotic Ectodermal Dysplasia is most characteristic?
opts: Decreased or absent eccrine sweat glands with normal hair follicles
Normal epidermis and normal eccrine/sebaceous glands but absent or rudimentary hair follicles
Pemphigus-like acantholysis with circulating anti-desmoglein antibodies
Lichenoid infiltrate with increased melanin at the dermal-epidermal junction
questions.exp: In Hidrotic Ectodermal Dysplasia, skin biopsies show a completely normal epidermis with normal distribution of eccrine sweat glands and sebaceous glands, but demonstrable absence or mere remnants of hair follicles. This normal sweat gland function is the defining histological distinction from Hypohidrotic Ectodermal Dysplasia.

questions.q: A 6-year-old unvaccinated boy presents with a 3-day history of high fever, coryza, conjunctivitis, and barking cough. On examination, you note bright red macules with blue-white centers on the buccal mucosa opposite the premolar teeth. What is the pathognomonic enanthem being described?
opts: Fordyce spots
Koplik's spots
Petechiae
Erythema multiforme
questions.exp: Koplik's spots are the pathognomonic enanthem of measles, appearing as tiny bright red macules with 1–2 mm blue-white ('grains of sand') centers on the buccal mucosa, typically opposite the premolar teeth. They appear 48 hours before the characteristic morbilliform exanthem and are highly specific for measles diagnosis.

questions.q: A 2-month-old male neonate of Nigerian descent presents with a poorly circumscribed, slate-gray macular patch measuring 8 cm over the lumbosacral region and buttocks. The parents are reassured about the lesion's natural history. Which optical phenomenon best explains the characteristic bluish hue of this lesion?
opts: Rayleigh scattering of longer wavelengths by superficial epidermal melanin
Tyndall effect causing selective scattering of shorter blue light wavelengths by deep dermal melanin
Mie scattering from collagen bundles in the reticular dermis
Absorption of red and green wavelengths by hemoglobin in dermal capillaries
questions.exp: The bluish-gray appearance of classic Mongolian spots results from the Tyndall effect, where shorter blue light wavelengths are scattered by melanin granules located in the deep dermal melanocytes and reflected back to the observer's eye. This optical illusion is specific to lesions in the mid and lower reticular dermis, explaining why the color appears blue rather than brown or black.

questions.q: A 2-month-old girl presents with linear atrophic skin lesions following the lines of Blaschko on her trunk and extremities. Her dermatologist suspects Focal Dermal Hypoplasia (Goltz Syndrome). Which of the following best explains why approximately 90% of affected patients are female?
opts: Females have two X chromosomes allowing functional mosaicism through X-inactivation, whereas hemizygous males with the mutation typically die in utero
The PORCN gene is preferentially expressed in female skin and causes earlier symptom manifestation in males
Males have stronger Wnt signaling that compensates for PORCN mutations, while females lack this protective mechanism
Female hormones enhance the penetrance of X-linked dominant disorders, making them more viable in utero
questions.exp: Goltz Syndrome is caused by X-linked dominant mutations in the PORCN gene on chromosome Xp11.23. In females, random X-chromosome inactivation (lyonization) creates a functional mosaicism with a mixture of normal and defective cells, allowing survival. In contrast, hemizygous males (46,XY) with the germline mutation typically experience intrauterine lethality, making live-born males extremely rare (~10% of cases). Surviving males require either somatic mosaicism or Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY).
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine 90 FEMALE WARRIORS standing guard at the castle gate, while MALE HEMIZYGOTES lie dead in the moat below—only the MOSAICKED (patchy X-inactivation) females survive the lethal X-linked dominant PORCN mutation.

questions.q: A 2-day-old neonate presents with a round, punched-out scalp defect covered by a thin, shiny, translucent epithelial membrane surrounded by a ring of dark, coarse, radially oriented hair. Which of the following best describes the embryological mechanism and key clinical sign?
opts: Non-membranous ACC from intrauterine vascular ischemia; associated with hypertrophic scarring
Membranous ACC from incomplete closure of embryonic ectodermal fusion lines; 'hair collar sign' is pathognomonic for possible underlying neural tube defect
Membranous ACC from placental infarction; 'hair collar sign' indicates Adams-Oliver syndrome
Non-membranous ACC from tension-induced disruption; 'hair collar sign' is always associated with cleft palate
questions.exp: Membranous ACC arises from incomplete closure of embryonic ectodermal fusion lines and characteristically presents as a round/oval translucent defect. The pathognomonic 'hair collar sign'—a ring of dark, coarse, radially oriented hair—is a clinical marker for an underlying neural tube defect. Non-membranous ACC results from vascular ischemia and presents as larger, irregular, stellate lesions with hypertrophic scarring, not membranous defects.

questions.q: A 4-year-old child with confirmed measles develops a nonpruritic, erythematous, blanching maculopapular rash. The rash initially appears behind the ears and on the forehead, then progresses over 2–4 days to the neck, trunk, and extremities. Which direction does the exanthem characteristically spread?
opts: Centripetal (center to periphery)
Caudocephalic (feet to head)
Cephalocaudal (head to toe)
Random distribution across all body areas simultaneously
questions.exp: The measles exanthem progresses in a strict cephalocaudal (head-to-toe) direction, beginning behind the ears, forehead, and anterior hairline, then spreading to the neck, trunk, and extremities over 2–4 days. The rash fades in the exact order it appeared, leaving a coppery-brown discoloration and fine desquamation.

questions.q: Which of the following histological findings best distinguishes frictional lichenoid eruption from true lichen planus?
opts: Dense band-like lymphocytic infiltrate along the dermoepidermal junction with basal cell destruction
Mild spongiotic dermatitis with hyperkeratosis and superficial perivascular infiltrate, without significant basal layer involvement
Follicular hyperkeratosis with spine-like keratin projections
Epidermal necrosis with subepidermal blister formation
questions.exp: Frictional lichenoid eruption shows mild, non-specific spongiotic dermatitis (intercellular edema), hyperkeratosis, and focal parakeratosis with a mild superficial perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate, but does NOT display the characteristic band-like lichenoid interface dermatitis or basal cell destruction seen in true lichen planus. This histological difference is crucial despite the misleading name "lichenoid."
questions.🏰 Palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a CASTLE MOAT (dermis) with GENTLE RIPPLES (spongiosis) and SHALLOW GUARDS standing in the SHALLOW END (superficial infiltrate)—not the DEEP, THICK WALL (band-like) that TRUE LICHEN PLANUS builds to DESTROY the CASTLE GATE (basal layer).

questions.q: A 3-week-old girl with incontinentia pigmenti presents with vesiculobullous lesions following a febrile illness. Her complete blood count shows marked leukocytosis and eosinophilia. What is the pathognomonic histopathological finding in Stage 1 lesions of incontinentia pigmenti?
opts: Eosinophilic spongiosis with scattered dyskeratotic keratinocytes
Subepidermal bullae with linear IgG deposits at the basement membrane zone
Dermal melanin incontinence with pigment-laden macrophages
Superficial dermal edema with neutrophilic infiltrate and fragmented nuclei
questions.exp: Stage 1 (vesiculobullous stage) of incontinentia pigmenti is characterized by eosinophilic spongiosis with scattered dyskeratotic (apoptotic) keratinocytes within the epidermis. This histological finding is universally accompanied by profound peripheral blood leukocytosis and eosinophilia in neonates, reflecting the widespread cellular apoptosis occurring in stage 1.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: An EOSINOPHIL SPONGE (soaking up stage 1 blisters) sits in the castle kitchen alongside DYSKERATOTIC GHOSTS (dying keratinocytes) haunting the epidermal walls.

questions.q: A 3-year-old boy presents with polymorphic reddish-brown macules and papules on his trunk and thighs. Stroking a lesion produces immediate localized whealing and erythema. Histopathology shows 40-fold increase in mast cells in the papillary dermis with increased basal melanin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Systemic mastocytosis with skin involvement
Maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis (urticaria pigmentosa)
Mastocytoma of skin
Telangiectasia macularis eruptiva perstans
questions.exp: Maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis (urticaria pigmentosa) is the most common form of cutaneous mastocytosis, presenting with reddish-brown lesions on trunk/thighs sparing face/palms/soles. Children characteristically show a polymorphic variant with larger lesions that resolve by adolescence. The positive Darier's sign (immediate whealing upon stroking) is the key distinguishing clinical feature due to mast cell degranulation.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a CHILD climbing pigmented STAIRS (UP = Urticaria Pigmentosa) on the TRUNK—when the stairs are stroked, they WHEEZE and WEAL (Darier's sign), releasing histamine like an angry wizard's spell.

questions.q: A 6-year-old boy presents with early-onset poikiloderma, hypoplastic thumbs, and absent radii. Genetic testing confirms compound heterozygous mutations in the RECQL4 gene. Which of the following statements is MOST accurate regarding his malignancy risk?
opts: He has a 32% lifetime risk of developing osteosarcoma and requires regular oncologic surveillance
He has no increased malignancy risk as RECQL4 mutations only affect skeletal development
He is exclusively at risk for melanoma due to the poikilodermic skin changes
His malignancy risk is limited to cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma only
questions.exp: RTS Type II, caused by RECQL4 mutations, confers a profound 32% lifetime risk of osteosarcoma alongside increased risk for cutaneous squamous and basal cell carcinomas. This represents the hallmark malignancy predisposition that distinguishes Type II from Type I disease. The skeletal abnormalities (radial ray defects, hypoplastic thumbs) are the clinical clue that identifies this high-risk subtype.

questions.q: Which molecular pathway is disrupted by loss-of-function mutations in the PORCN gene in Focal Dermal Hypoplasia, and what is the primary structural consequence in skin?
opts: Wnt signaling pathway; profound dermal thinning with subcutaneous fat herniation upward and adnexal dysplasia
Notch signaling pathway; excessive dermal fibrosis with impaired epidermal-dermal adhesion
TGF-β signaling pathway; increased collagen deposition causing skin thickening and pigmentation changes
FGF signaling pathway; selective destruction of hair follicles with preservation of dermal integrity
questions.exp: The PORCN protein is essential for membrane targeting and secretion of Wnt proteins, which are critical for normal embryonic development of mesodermal and ectodermal tissues. Loss-of-function PORCN mutations disrupt Wnt signaling, leading to failure of dermal connective tissue formation. This results in extreme dermal thinning, allowing subcutaneous fat to herniate upward directly abutting the epidermis, along with severe dysplasia of ectodermal adnexal structures including hair follicles, teeth, and nails.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture the castle's STONE WALLS (dermal collagen) crumbling because the WNT-carrying PORTERS (PORCN protein) abandoned their posts—fat pillows then BULGE through the gaps like herniated cushions bursting through broken ramparts.

questions.q: A 6-month-old female of mixed ethnicity presents with extensive, dark Mongolian spots involving the trunk, shoulders, extremities, and ventral trunk with a confetti-like appearance. She exhibits developmental delay and hepatosplenomegaly on examination. Which inborn error of metabolism is most likely to be associated with this extensive presentation?
opts: Acute intermittent porphyria
Gaucher disease (lysosomal lipid storage only)
Hurler's disease (MPS I) or Hunter's disease (MPS II)
Familial hypercholesterolemia
questions.exp: Extensive, dark, and progressive Mongolian spots are a major cutaneous red flag for inborn errors of metabolism, particularly lysosomal storage diseases such as Hurler's disease (MPS I) and Hunter's disease (MPS II). The combination of extensive dermal melanocytosis with systemic features like developmental delay and hepatosplenomegaly strongly suggests an underlying metabolic disorder.

questions.q: A dermatopathology slide shows a dense lymphohistiocytic perivascular infiltrate with pathognomonic wedge-shaped extensions pointing downward into the reticular dermis, marked basal cell vacuolization with exocytosis of CD8+ T-cells, and confluent parakeratosis with necrotic keratinocytes. Which histological feature is ABSENT in this case of PLEVA?
opts: Fibrinoid necrosis of blood vessel walls
Extravasated erythrocytes within the epidermis
Wedge-shaped dermal infiltrate
Basal cell vacuolization and interface dermatitis
questions.exp:
PLEVA is characterized by a dense perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate with wedge-shaped extensions, marked basal cell vacuolization, exocytosis of CD8+ T-cells, and confluent parakeratosis with necrotic keratinocytes, but it classically LACKS true fibrinoid necrosis of the blood vessel walls. This distinguishes it from some other vasculitic and interface dermatoses.
🏰 Palace: In the PLEVA castle, the BLOOD VESSEL WALLS remain INTACT and UNFIBRINIZED—the lymphocytes attack the SURROUNDING TISSUE, not the vessels themselves. NO fibrin ropes tying down the vessels!

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with clusters of small, discrete, flat-topped papules on his elbows and knees that appeared after a week of playing outdoors in sand during summer. The papules are asymptomatic to mildly pruritic and 1–2 mm in size. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Lichen planus
Frictional lichenoid eruption
Lichen nitidus with systemic sclerosis
Pityriasis rubra pilaris
questions.exp: Frictional lichenoid eruption (FLE) characteristically presents as 1–2 mm discrete papules on the elbows and knees, triggered by minor frictional trauma (sand, grass, carpets) during warm months in children aged 4–12 years. The extensor surfaces of extremities are the classic distribution site due to frictional contact. Unlike true lichen planus, FLE shows non-specific spongiotic dermatitis on histology rather than band-like lichenoid interface changes.
questions.🏰 Palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine a SEVEN-YEAR-OLD BOY (7) crawling through SAND and GRASS in SUMMER, collecting tiny PAPULES like GRAINS OF SAND on his ELBOWS and KNEES—friction turns his play zone into a friction zone.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with an abrupt eruption of small erythematous papules with central vesiculation, necrosis, and hemorrhagic crusting affecting his trunk and extremities. The lesions appear in different stages of development simultaneously. Which immunological mechanism best explains the pathogenesis of this condition?
opts: IgG and IgA antibody deposition against basement membrane antigens
CD8+ cytotoxic T-lymphocyte–mediated cellular immunity triggered by an exogenous antigen
IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation in response to allergens
Circulating immune complex deposition in dermal blood vessels
questions.exp:
PLEVA (Pityriasis Lichenoides et Varioliformis Acuta), also known as Mucha-Habermann Disease, is a T-cell–mediated lymphoproliferative disorder driven entirely by CD8+ cytotoxic T-lymphocytes (expressing TIA-1 and granzyme B) responding to exogenous triggers, particularly preceding viral or bacterial infections. It is NOT antibody-mediated and involves no pathogenic immunoglobulins or circulating immune complexes.
🏰 Palace: Picture a TOXIC CD8+ KNIGHT (cytotoxic T-cell) storming the castle's BASAL WALL (epidermal basal layer) with GRANULE WEAPONS (granzyme B/TIA-1), leaving NECROTIC RUBBLE—no IgG knights needed!

questions.q: A 2-month-old White non-Hispanic female infant born at 28 weeks gestation (birth weight 1200 g) and her first-degree relative both have infantile haemangiomas. Genetic counselling is sought. Which chromosomal region and associated gene are implicated in familial infantile haemangioma susceptibility?
opts: Chromosome 12q with KIT mutations
Chromosome 5q with VEGFR2 and ANTXR1 mutations
Chromosome Xp with PTEN aberrations
Chromosome 17p with TP53 inactivation
questions.exp: Linkage studies in familial infantile haemangioma kindreds map a susceptibility locus to chromosome 5q. Heterozygous germline mutations in VEGFR2 and ANTXR1 (encoding TEM8) have been identified in affected families and also in sporadic cases as predisposing factors. The other chromosomal aberrations are associated with different genetic syndromes.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: A FIVE-POINTED STAR (chromosome 5q) hangs above GRANDMOTHER'S FAMILY MANOR, where VEGF KNIGHTS and ANTXR1 SENTRIES pass down the PROLIFERATION CURSE through generations—each heir inheriting the vascular treasure map.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with a solitary, sharply demarcated, jet-black macule measuring 4 mm on her left thigh. Dermoscopy reveals a distinctive pattern of a dark structureless center surrounded by symmetric radiating pigmented streaks. Histology shows tightly aggregated fascicles of heavily pigmented spindle cells arranged vertically within the dermal-epidermal junction, sparing the deep reticular dermis. Which of the following best describes this lesion?
opts: Classic pigmented spindle cell nevus (Reed nevus) with characteristic junctional architecture
Spitz nevus with epithelioid cell predominance
Plexiform spindle cell nevus with reticular dermal extension
Superficial cutaneous melanoma with spindle cell morphology
questions.exp: The clinical presentation (young adult female, thigh location), dermoscopic starburst pattern, and histologic features (junctional/superficial papillary dermis involvement, spindle cells, symmetric plate-like configuration) are pathognomonic for classic Reed nevus. The sparing of the deep reticular dermis and absence of epithelioid cells distinguish it from other Spitz lineage variants and melanoma.

questions.q: A young adult presents with symmetric edema, erythema, and petechiae confined strictly to the dorsal hands and feet with an abrupt sharp demarcation at the wrists and ankles. Oral enanthem is noted on the soft palate and buccal mucosa. Which parvovirus B19-associated syndrome is this, and which age group is typically affected?
opts: Papular-Purpuric Gloves and Socks Syndrome (PPGSS); young adults
Classic Erythema Infectiosum; school-aged children aged 4–10 years
Hydrops Fetalis; pregnant women in second trimester
Arthropathy syndrome; elderly patients over 60 years
questions.exp: PPGSS is a distinct acral variant of parvovirus B19 characterized by sharply demarcated symmetric involvement of the distal hands and feet with purpuric papules and enanthem, predominantly affecting young adults rather than school-aged children. Skin biopsy shows viral structural proteins in dermal blood vessel walls.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine GLOVES and SOCKS made of PURPLE GLITTER being put on a YOUNG ADULT'S hands and feet at the ballroom—the SHARP LINE at the WRIST and ANKLE acts like a CASTLE MOAT separating the affected acral zones from normal skin above.

questions.q: A 9-year-old girl with vitiligo is found to have elevated anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies and subclinical hypothyroidism on screening. This autoimmune comorbidity is best explained by which genetic and immunopathological basis?
opts: Polygenic susceptibility with shared HLA risk loci and immune dysregulation genes (PTPN22, NALP1) that predispose to multiple autoimmune endocrinopathies
Molecular mimicry between melanocyte tyrosinase and thyroid peroxidase epitopes leading to cross-reactive CD4+ T cells
IFN-γ and CXCL10 chemokine-mediated direct destruction of thyroid tissue identical to melanocyte targeting
Segmental vitiligo inheritance pattern that genetically predetermines autoimmune thyroid disease
questions.exp: Vitiligo is a polygenic disorder with approximately 50 susceptibility loci identified by GWAS, the vast majority encoding immune-regulatory proteins including HLA genes and genes such as PTPN22, NALP1, and IFIH1. This shared genetic architecture with autoimmune endocrinopathies results in strong clinical associations with Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Type 1 Diabetes, Addison's disease, and other autoimmune conditions. Childhood vitiligo shows particularly strong association with family history of autoimmune diseases and atopic diathesis.

questions.q: A 7-year-old child presents with a bright red, confluent macular erythema strictly localized to the cheeks with sparing of the nasal bridge and circumoral regions. One to three days later, a lacy, reticulated eruption appears on the extremities and trunk. What is the causative agent and the classic name for this cutaneous presentation?
opts: Human Parvovirus B19; 'Slapped Cheek' Disease
Measles virus; 'Morbilliform' eruption
Rubella virus; 'Punctate' exanthem
Varicella-zoster virus; 'Vesicular' eruption
questions.exp: Fifth disease (erythema infectiosum) is caused by Human Parvovirus B19 and classically presents with a 'slapped cheek' appearance followed by a lacy, reticulated rash on the trunk and extremities. The patient is no longer infectious once the cutaneous rash appears, distinguishing it from measles and other viral exanthems.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a CHILD'S CHEEK being SLAPPED BRIGHT RED by a giant PARVOVIRUS B19 (shaped like a LACY GLOVE) at the castle entrance—the face gets hit FIRST (days 4–15), then the glove-hands reach out to the ARMS and THIGHS.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child with naevus spilus is found to have a postzygotic somatic mutation causing a localized 'field defect' of melanocytes. Which of the following best explains the pathophysiological mechanism and why this condition lacks specific autoimmune features?
opts: Autosomal dominant germline BRCA1 mutation with HLA-B27 association leading to chronic immune activation
Postzygotic somatic HRAS mutation creating a susceptible hamartomatous field, not driven by immune-mediated attack or autoantigens
X-linked recessive mutation in PTEN with loss of immune tolerance and anti-melanocyte antibodies
Polygenic inheritance involving multiple HLA loci with aberrant T-cell recognition of melanocytic self-antigens
questions.exp: Naevus spilus is a benign melanocytic neoplasm and mosaic genodermatosis caused by postzygotic somatic mutations—classically HRAS c.37G→C (p.Gly13Arg)—creating a localized hamartomatous proliferation. Because it is an embryological anomaly driven by genetic field defect rather than autoimmune pathology, it completely lacks autoimmune receptors, autoantigens, or HLA associations. The mutation drives neural crest-derived melanocyte proliferation, not immune-mediated destruction.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: A SOMATIC SEED (postzygotic mutation—one cell divides!) plants an HRAS GARDEN (field defect) in the MELANOCYTE MEADOW; no IMMUNE GUARDS (no HLA, no autoantigen gatekeepers) patrol this HAMARTOMA HAMLET because it's a benign CONSTRUCTION CREW (proliferation), not an AUTOIMMUNE INVASION (attack).

questions.q: A 8-month-old infant presents with a light-brown patch on the trunk with superimposed flat dark specks distributed in a uniform polka-dot pattern. Histology shows lentiginous melanocytic hyperplasia along the basal layer with dark speckles confined to the dermal-epidermal junction at the tips of rete ridges. Which naevus spilus variant is this, and what is its key syndromic association?
opts: Naevus spilus papulosus associated with phakomatosis pigmentokeratotica
Naevus spilus maculosus associated with phakomatosis spilorosea
Naevus spilus papulosus associated with phakomatosis spilorosea
Naevus spilus maculosus associated with phakomatosis pigmentokeratotica
questions.exp: The flat (macular) dark speckles with uniform polka-dot pattern and histology confined to the epidermal-junctional layer define naevus spilus maculosus. This variant is the hallmark cutaneous finding in phakomatosis spilorosea (historically type IIIb), which also includes a nevus flammeus and sometimes a nevus anemicus. The papular variant with star-map appearance and dermal extension is instead associated with phakomatosis pigmentokeratotica.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Picture a MACULAR MACARON (flat cookie sprinkles—polka dots!) in a SPILOROSEA CASTLE where PORT-WINE stains decorate the walls; the PAPULAR PAPRIKA (bumpy spice clusters—star map!) lives next door in PIGMENTOKERATOTICA PALACE with its sebaceous neighbor.

questions.q: A 3-week-old infant with aplasia cutis congenita on the scalp undergoes investigation and is found to have terminal transverse limb defects, cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita, and a ventriculoseptal defect. Which gene mutation is LEAST likely to be causative in this autosomal dominant presentation?
opts: ARHGAP31
BMS1
RBPJ
NOTCH1
questions.exp: The clinical presentation of scalp ACC with limb reduction abnormalities and cardiac malformations is diagnostic of Adams-Oliver Syndrome (Group 2 ACC). BMS1 mutations are associated with isolated Group 1 scalp ACC without multiple anomalies. Adams-Oliver Syndrome in autosomal dominant cases results from mutations in ARHGAP31, RBPJ, NOTCH1, or DLL4, none of which is BMS1.

questions.q: Regarding the pathogenesis of Reed nevus, which of the following statements is CORRECT?
opts: Reed nevus is driven by autoimmune destruction of melanocytes mediated by specific IgG autoantibodies against melanocytic antigens
The lesion arises from somatic mutations within the MAPK signaling cascade, such as HRAS mutations or kinase fusions, independent of immune-mediated mechanisms
Reed nevus pathogenesis is primarily associated with strong HLA-B8 and HLA-DR3 haplotypes characteristic of autoimmune bullous disorders
The condition results from impaired T-regulatory cell function leading to chronic antigenic stimulation of dermal lymphocytes
questions.exp: Reed nevus is a benign hamartomatous/neoplastic proliferation of melanocytes driven entirely by somatic genetic events (HRAS mutations, kinase fusions) within the MAPK pathway. It is NOT an autoimmune or immunobullous disorder and therefore lacks pathogenic antibody isotypes, targeted autoantigens, or characteristic HLA associations.

questions.q: Which receptor mutation is found in approximately 80–90% of adult mastocytosis patients but only 42% of pediatric cases?
opts: E839K mutation in exon 8
D816V mutation in exon 17 of KIT gene
TET2 mutation in advanced systemic mastocytosis
RUNX1 mutation associated with poor prognosis
questions.exp: The D816V point mutation in exon 17 of the KIT proto-oncogene is the classic somatic mutation found in 80–90% of adult mastocytosis cases. In contrast, children show greater genetic diversity, with only 42% harboring D816V and 44% carrying mutations in extracellular/transmembrane domains (exons 8–11) or rare inactivating mutations like E839K.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine an ADULT DICTATOR (80–90%) sitting on exon 17's THRONE (D816V), while CHILDREN roam freely in the castle's outer WINGS (exons 8–11) with diverse rebellious mutations—D816V is the TYRANT of adulthood.

questions.q: A 7-year-old girl with Rothmund-Thomson syndrome develops bilateral cataracts requiring surgical intervention. Her genetic testing reveals ANAPC1 gene mutations. What is the most important counseling point regarding her future malignancy screening?
opts: She requires intensive osteosarcoma surveillance given the 32% risk associated with ANAPC1 mutations
She has NO increased incidence of malignancy and does not require cancer-specific dermatologic or oncologic screening beyond standard pediatric care
She is at high risk for basal cell carcinoma and requires monthly skin examinations
She requires genetic testing of first-degree relatives to assess their malignancy risk
questions.exp: RTS Type I, caused by ANAPC1 mutations, presents classically with juvenile cataracts (the original Rothmund presentation) but crucially carries NO increased incidence of malignancy. This cancer-sparing profile is the critical distinguishing feature that separates Type I from the malignancy-prone Type II disease. Counseling should emphasize normal malignancy risk.

questions.q: A 3-month-old premature female infant (birth weight 800 g) presents with multiple small red papules on the trunk in a miliary pattern. Biopsy confirms infantile haemangioma. Which of the following is the most reliable immunohistochemical marker that distinguishes this lesion from congenital haemangiomas and vascular malformations?
opts: CD31 expression in endothelial cells
GLUT1 (glucose transporter-1) positivity throughout all phases of the life cycle
VEGF receptor upregulation only during the proliferative phase
Factor VIII-related antigen in vessel walls
questions.exp: GLUT1 is the universal hallmark of infantile haemangiomas, expressed by endothelial cells throughout proliferating, involuting, and involuted phases. This distinguishes IH from congenital haemangiomas and vascular malformations, which lack GLUT1 expression. CD31, VEGF receptors, and Factor VIII are not specific discriminators for IH.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a GLUCOSE TRUCK (GLUT1) delivering FUEL to BABY VAMPIRES (infantile haemangiomas) throughout their entire LIFESPAN—from birth (proliferation) through retirement (involution)—while the malformed vascular zombies next door get ZERO deliveries.

questions.q: A 7-year-old child presents with depigmented patches on the left side of the trunk that stop sharply at the midline and have not progressed over 18 months. Which histopathological finding would you expect on examination of a skin biopsy from the lesional margin?
opts: Complete absence of melanocytes in the basal layer with sparse CD8+ lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermoepidermal junction
Hyperplasia of melanocytes with increased melanin production in the basal layer
Dense neutrophilic infiltrate throughout the dermis with preserved melanocytes
Preservation of melanocytes but with reduced dendritic processes and abnormal MITF expression
questions.exp: Vitiligo is characterized by immune-mediated destruction of melanocytes. Histopathology shows a complete absence of melanocytes in the basal layer (confirmed by negative Melan-A/MART-1, MITF, HMB-45, or DOPA staining), and early active inflammatory margins display a sparse, band-like superficial CD8+ lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermoepidermal junction. The unilateral, midline-stopping pattern with stability suggests segmental vitiligo, which is uniquely prominent in childhood (15–30% of pediatric cases).
